title: Land Still to Be Taken, Land Already Given
summary: The LORD tells an aging Joshua that much land remains to be possessed, names those regions (Philistia, the coast toward Sidon, Lebanon), promises to drive out their peoples himself, and commands Joshua to divide the land by lot. The chapter then records the territories Moses had already given east of the Jordan to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, and notes twice that Levi received no land, because the LORD and his offerings were Levi's inheritance.
story: The book now turns from war to inheritance, and chapters 13-21 describe how the land was divided among the tribes. The turn begins honestly: Joshua is old, and the conquest is incomplete. The rest announced in 11:23 was real, but it did not mean that every Canaanite was gone or that every region was in Israel's hands. God's answer is not to wait until everything is taken but to divide the land now, trusting that he will finish what he began. Before describing the western allotments, the narrator reviews the eastern ones Moses had made (Numbers 32), so that all twelve tribes are accounted for.
historical:
The unconquered land in verses 2-6 lies mainly along the coast. The Philistines, with their five cities of Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron, held the southern coastal plain. Egyptian records from the reign of Ramesses III, in the early twelfth century BC, describe battles with groups called the Sea Peoples, among them the Peleset, generally identified with the Philistines. Scholars who date the conquest early often see the Philistines of Joshua as earlier settlers or the name as an updating by a later writer; those who date it later see less difficulty. Further north lay the Phoenician coast of Sidon and the land of the Gebalites, the people of Byblos, a major port in what is now Lebanon.

The eastern territories include places known from outside the Bible. Dibon (modern Dhiban in Jordan) is where the Mesha Stele was discovered in 1868; in that ninth-century BC inscription, King Mesha of Moab claims to have taken towns north of the Arnon, including Medeba, and mentions the men of Gad living in Ataroth. An inscription found in 1967 at Deir Alla in the Jordan Valley, from around the eighth century BC, speaks of Balaam son of Beor as a seer, showing that his name was remembered in the region. Geshur, which Israel did not drive out (verse 13), later appears as the kingdom of David's father-in-law Talmai (2 Samuel 3:3).
cultural:
Inheritance (nachalah) was the heart of Israelite identity. Land in Israel was not a commodity to be bought and sold permanently but a family's share of the LORD's land, handed down through generations. Leviticus 25:23 says the land belongs to the LORD and Israel lives on it as foreigners and sojourners. Dividing the land by lot, as verse 6 commands, placed the decision in God's hands and prevented the strongest tribes from seizing the best ground. The references to clans in each tribe show that the land was allotted down to extended families.

The tribe of Levi was set apart for the service of the tabernacle. Instead of a territory, they received the priestly share of the offerings brought to the LORD and, as chapter 21 will describe, towns to live in scattered through all the tribes. Verse 14 says the offerings made by fire were their inheritance; verse 33 says the LORD himself was. The two statements say the same thing from two sides.
literary: The chapter is built from a divine speech (verses 1-7) and a geographical record (verses 8-33). The speech names what remains before it commands the division, placing the unfinished and the promised side by side. The record then moves tribe by tribe: Reuben (verses 15-23), Gad (verses 24-28), and the half-tribe of Manasseh (verses 29-31), each section opening with “This is what Moses had given” and closing with a summary line. The note about Levi appears twice (verses 14 and 33), framing the eastern allotments, and the brief notes about Geshur and Balaam add small stories to the map: an unfinished task, and the end of the prophet who had tried to curse Israel (Numbers 22-24; 31:8).

outline.t: The LORD's charge to an old Joshua: land remains, divide it
The eastern lands Moses gave, and Levi's portion
The inheritance of half of Manasseh, and Levi again

doctrines.note: The land is given as inheritance, a gift within the covenant. God commands Israel to divide land it does not yet fully hold, because the promise rests on his word: “I Myself will drive out before the Israelites” (verse 6).

Levi's lack of land marks the tribe as set apart for God. Its members depend directly on the LORD and on the worship of the people, a living reminder that Israel's life centered on God rather than on property.

The brief note on Balaam's death (verse 22) recalls that the prophet who could not curse Israel later led it into sin at Peor (Numbers 31:16). Judgment catches up with those who oppose God's people, even when it is delayed.

words.note: Nachalah, inheritance. The word appears nine times in this chapter and dominates the second half of Joshua. It means a share passed down within a family, and it presents the land as a gift from the LORD received as his children, not as plunder. For Levi, the inheritance is the LORD himself.

Yarash, to take possession, often by dispossessing others. The LORD says that very much land remains “to be possessed.” The word holds together God's gift and Israel's responsibility to take hold of it.

Mishpachah, clan or family. Larger than a household and smaller than a tribe, the clan was the unit that actually received and worked the land. Its repetition shows that the promise reached down to ordinary families.

christ: The link is thematic, and it runs through the idea of inheritance. Levi's inheritance was the LORD himself, and the Psalms take up this language for every faithful believer (Psalm 16:5-6; 73:26). The New Testament widens the promise of land into an inheritance of the whole renewed creation: Jesus says the meek will inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5), and Peter speaks of an inheritance kept in heaven that can never perish (1 Peter 1:4). In Christ, believers are called fellow heirs (Romans 8:17), and like Levi they are called to priestly service, a royal priesthood and a people belonging to God (1 Peter 2:9).
questions: God told an old man that much work remained, and then told him to divide the land anyway. How do you act on God's promises when the work looks unfinished?
For Levi, the LORD himself was the inheritance. What would it mean for you to treat God, rather than any possession or position, as your portion?
Israel did not drive out Geshur, and Geshur shows up again in David's troubled family. What small compromises have had long consequences in your life or community?
